stem: What does a farmer use a **herbicide** for?

options.content: To kill insects that eat the crop
options.rationale: That is an insecticide.

options.content: To kill weeds that compete with the crop
options.rationale: Herbicides kill unwanted plants.

options.content: To supply mineral ions to the crop
options.rationale: That is a fertiliser.

options.content: To kill fungi that cause crop diseases
options.rationale: That is a fungicide.

explanation: Herbicides kill weeds, which compete with crops for light, water, mineral ions and space. Insecticides kill insects and fungicides kill fungi.

stem: What is a **monoculture**?

options.content: A farm that keeps only one type of animal indoors
options.rationale: That describes intensive livestock production.

options.content: Growing several different crops in the same field at the same time
options.rationale: That is mixed cropping (intercropping), the opposite of a monoculture.

options.content: A crop grown from a single seed
options.rationale: Monoculture refers to the whole area planted, not to one seed.

options.content: Growing a single crop species over a large area
options.rationale: For example, thousands of hectares of sugar cane or maize.

explanation: A monoculture is a large area planted with one crop species, often the same variety and often year after year.

stem: Name the type of chemical that farmers spray to kill the **insects** that damage their crops.

rejected.feedback: Insecticides are one kind of pesticide; the question asks for the kind that kills insects.
Herbicides kill weeds. Insect pests are killed by insecticides.
Fungicides kill fungi. Insect pests are killed by insecticides.
Fertilisers supply mineral ions. Insect pests are killed by insecticides.

explanation: Insecticides kill insect pests such as fall armyworm, stalk borers, aphids and bollworms, so less of the crop is lost. Herbicides kill weeds and fungicides kill fungi.
hints: The first part of the word refers to the organisms it kills.

stem: True or false: selective breeding can produce a new, high-yielding crop variety in a single generation.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Not so: selective breeding needs many generations of choosing the best plants, breeding them and selecting again from their offspring.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: Correct: selective breeding takes many generations, choosing the best individuals as parents each time.

explanation: In selective breeding, people choose parents with useful features, breed them, select the best offspring and repeat. The features build up gradually over many generations.
hints: How many rounds of choosing parents are usually needed?

stem: How do chemical fertilisers increase crop yields?

options.content: They supply the glucose that the crop uses for energy
options.rationale: Plants make their own glucose by photosynthesis.

options.content: They kill the pests that eat the crop
options.rationale: That is the job of insecticides.

options.content: They supply mineral ions, such as nitrate, that the soil has lost
options.rationale: Nitrate is used to make amino acids and proteins for growth.

options.content: They supply extra carbon dioxide to the leaves for photosynthesis
options.rationale: Plants take carbon dioxide from the air; fertilisers supply mineral ions.

explanation: Each harvest removes mineral ions from the soil. Fertilisers replace them; for example, nitrate is used to make amino acids and proteins, and magnesium to make chlorophyll, so the crop grows more.

stem: Match each farming method with the way it increases food production.

right.content: Lets fewer workers plant and harvest larger areas quickly
Replaces mineral ions removed from the soil
Kills insects that eat or damage the crop
Kills weeds that compete for light, water and mineral ions
Produces varieties with higher yields or resistance to disease over many generations
Kills fungi that cause plant diseases

explanation: Machinery increases the area farmed and speeds up the work; fertilisers replace mineral ions; insecticides and herbicides reduce losses to insects and weeds; selective breeding improves varieties. Killing fungi is the job of a fungicide, which is not in the list.
hints: One description belongs to a different kind of pesticide.

stem: Why do weeds growing among a maize crop reduce its yield?

options.content: They compete with the maize for light, water, ions and space
options.rationale: Every weed uses resources that the crop could have used.

options.content: They release oxygen, which harms the maize leaves
options.rationale: Weeds do photosynthesise, but the oxygen does not harm the crop.

options.content: They eat the maize plants
options.rationale: Weeds are plants; they do not eat other plants.

options.content: They take all the carbon dioxide out of the soil around the roots
options.rationale: Plants take carbon dioxide from the air, and this does not explain the lost yield.

explanation: Weeds are plants growing where they are not wanted. They compete with the crop for light, water, mineral ions and space, so the crop grows less.

stem: Which of these is a **disadvantage** of growing tobacco as a large monoculture year after year?

options.content: The same machinery can be used across the whole farm
options.rationale: This is an advantage: it makes farming efficient.

options.content: Pests and diseases of tobacco build up and spread quickly through the crop
options.rationale: A huge area of one host plant, year after year, lets pest populations grow.

options.content: The crop is uniform, so it is easy to harvest and sell
options.rationale: This is an advantage.

options.content: The farmer can specialise and become very skilled at growing and curing one crop
options.rationale: This is an advantage.

explanation: A monoculture provides a large, continuous food supply for the pests and diseases of that crop, so they build up and spread, especially if the same crop is grown on the same land every year.
hints: Three of the options are advantages.

stem: Broiler chickens kept in a warm house, where they move very little, gain more mass from each kilogram of feed than free-range chickens. Why?

options.content: They respire faster, releasing more energy
options.rationale: Faster respiration would use more food, not less.

options.content: Their food contains no fibre, so they digest all of it
options.rationale: The diet matters, but this does not explain the efficiency compared with free-range birds.

options.content: Less food energy goes on moving and keeping warm, so more goes on growth
options.rationale: Less energy lost means more is available to build body mass.

options.content: They absorb heat energy from the heaters directly through their skin
options.rationale: Animals gain energy from food, not by absorbing heat from heaters.

explanation: An animal uses energy from its food for movement and to keep its body warm. Keeping broilers warm and inactive reduces these losses, so a larger share of the energy in the feed ends up as body mass.
hints: Where does the energy in an animal's food go?

stem: Select **all** the disadvantages of intensive livestock production.

options.content: Large amounts of manure collect in one place and can pollute water
options.rationale: Concentrated waste can run off into rivers and dams.

options.content: Meat and eggs cost more to produce
options.rationale: Intensive production usually makes them cheaper.

options.content: Diseases spread quickly between crowded animals
options.rationale: Close contact lets pathogens pass easily from animal to animal.

options.content: The animals have little space to move or behave naturally
options.rationale: This is a welfare concern.

options.content: Each animal needs more land than on a free-range farm
options.rationale: Intensive units use less land per animal.

options.content: The animals use more energy to keep warm
options.rationale: They are usually kept warm, so they use less energy keeping warm.

explanation: Intensive units save land and produce food cheaply, but crowding spreads disease (and leads to heavy antibiotic use), waste is concentrated, and the animals have little space or natural behaviour.
hints: Three of the statements are untrue: intensive farming actually has the opposite effect.

stem: On a farm near Bindura, maize grown without fertiliser yielded $0.8$ tonnes per hectare. On a similar field where fertiliser was used, the yield was $2.6$ tonnes per hectare. Calculate the percentage increase in yield.
explanation: Increase $= 2.6 - 0.8 = 1.8$ tonnes per hectare. Percentage increase $= 1.8 \div 0.8 \times 100 = 225\%$.
workedSolution:
1. Increase $= 2.6 - 0.8 = 1.8$ t/ha
2. Percentage increase $= \dfrac{1.8}{0.8} \times 100 = 225\%$ (divide by the **original** yield)

stem: Complete the description of how a breeder could produce a drought-tolerant maize variety.

payload.template: The breeder chooses parent plants that {{blank:feature}} and cross-breeds them. From the offspring, she {{blank:select}} the plants that survive dry conditions best. She repeats this for {{blank:generations}} generations.

explanation: Selective breeding: choose parents with the wanted feature (good growth with little water), breed them, select the best offspring and repeat over many generations until the variety reliably shows the feature.

stem: In some intensive pig and poultry units, antibiotics are given routinely to healthy animals. Why does this worry doctors?

options.content: The antibiotics make the meat grow too quickly
options.rationale: The concern is about bacteria, not about how fast the animals grow.

options.content: Antibiotics kill the helpful viruses that the animals need
options.rationale: Antibiotics act on bacteria, not viruses.

options.content: Antibiotics turn the harmless bacteria in the animals' guts into dangerous viruses
options.rationale: Bacteria cannot turn into viruses.

options.content: Resistant bacteria survive and spread, so the drugs may fail for people too
options.rationale: Overuse selects for resistant bacteria.

explanation: Every use of an antibiotic kills susceptible bacteria and leaves any resistant ones to multiply. Routine use in crowded animal units increases the chance that resistant strains develop and spread, including to people.
hints: Think about natural selection among bacteria.

stem:
A trial compared maize yields under four treatments on similar plots.

| Treatment | Yield / tonnes per hectare |
| --- | --- |
| No fertiliser, no herbicide | 1.0 |
| Herbicide only | 1.6 |
| Fertiliser only | 2.8 |
| Fertiliser and herbicide | 3.9 |

Which conclusion is supported by the results?

options.content: Fertiliser alone raised the yield more than herbicide alone did
options.rationale: Fertiliser added 1.8 t/ha; herbicide added 0.6 t/ha.

options.content: Herbicide alone had no effect at all on the yield of maize
options.rationale: Herbicide alone raised the yield from 1.0 to 1.6 t/ha.

options.content: Each treatment on its own doubled the yield
options.rationale: Herbicide alone gave 1.6 t/ha, not 2.0 t/ha.

options.content: Weeds do not compete with maize for anything
options.rationale: Controlling weeds raised the yield, so weeds were competing with the maize.

explanation: Compared with the untreated plot, fertiliser alone added $2.8 - 1.0 = 1.8$ t/ha and herbicide alone added $1.6 - 1.0 = 0.6$ t/ha. Together they gave the highest yield.
hints: Compare each treatment with the untreated plot.

stem: A farmer has sprayed the same herbicide on his large maize fields every season for many years. One weed species that the herbicide used to kill now survives the spray and is spreading through his fields. What is the **best** explanation?

options.content: The weeds have learned to close their stomata whenever they are sprayed
options.rationale: Plants do not learn; the change is inherited resistance.

options.content: The herbicide becomes weaker each time it is used
options.rationale: The chemical is the same; the weed population has changed.

options.content: A few resistant weeds survived each spraying and passed on their resistance
options.rationale: Repeated spraying with one herbicide is a strong selection pressure.

options.content: The maize plants have absorbed all the herbicide, so none reaches the weeds
options.rationale: This would not explain why only one weed species survives.

explanation: In a large weed population a few plants have variations that make them resistant. Repeated spraying kills the others, so the resistant plants survive, reproduce and pass on their resistance: natural selection. Growing the same crop with the same herbicide year after year, as in a monoculture, makes this more likely; rotating crops and herbicides helps to prevent it.
hints: Think of the weeds as a varied population facing a selection pressure.

stem: Large estates in the south-eastern Lowveld grow sugar cane over thousands of hectares, irrigated with water from dams. The cane is cut and taken to a nearby mill.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: State what is meant by a **monoculture**.

points.description: Growing a single crop species (or variety) over a large area

parts.explanation: A monoculture is a single crop species grown over a large area.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Suggest **two** advantages to the estate of growing only sugar cane.

points.description: One set of machinery and methods / efficient planting, spraying and harvesting
Large, uniform harvest that suits the mill / cheaper production per tonne / staff become specialists

parts.explanation: The estate needs only one set of machinery and methods, and it produces a large, uniform harvest that keeps the mill running cheaply.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain why pests and diseases can become a serious problem on the estate.

points.description: A large area of one host plant gives pests and pathogens a plentiful food supply / easy spread from plant to plant
Growing the crop year after year lets their numbers build up (no break in the cycle)

parts.explanation: The pests and pathogens of sugar cane have a huge, continuous food supply and can spread easily from plant to plant, and growing cane year after year lets their numbers build up.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: What is the most likely effect of replacing natural woodland with the estate on the number of species living in the area?

options.content: It increases, because sugar cane provides food
options.rationale: Few species can feed on sugar cane, and many lose their food and shelter.

options.content: It decreases, because there are fewer habitats and food sources
options.rationale: One crop replaces the many plants and habitats of the woodland.

options.content: It stays the same, because animals move into the cane
options.rationale: Most woodland species cannot live in a cane field.

options.content: It increases, because the irrigation water attracts more animals
options.rationale: A few species may benefit, but overall biodiversity falls.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Suggest **one** way in which the fertiliser used on the estate could harm the environment.

points.description: Runoff or leaching into rivers and dams causes water pollution / eutrophication (algal growth, loss of oxygen, death of fish)

parts.explanation: Fertiliser washed into rivers and dams can cause eutrophication: algae grow, then die and decompose, and oxygen levels fall so fish die.

explanation: A monoculture is efficient and suits large-scale processing, but it reduces biodiversity, encourages the build-up of pests and diseases, and relies heavily on fertilisers and pesticides that can pollute water.
workedSolution:
**(a)** One crop species over a large area.

**(b)** Efficient use of machinery and methods; large uniform harvest for the mill.

**(c)** Plentiful food supply for pests and pathogens; numbers build up year after year.

**(d)** Number of species decreases.

**(e)** Fertiliser runoff → eutrophication of rivers and dams.
hints: Think about what pests of sugar cane need to multiply.

stem: Tendai runs a broiler unit near Harare. In one six-week batch, each bird ate $3.6\ \text{kg}$ of feed on average and gained $2.1\ \text{kg}$ in mass.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the mass of feed needed for each kilogram of mass gained. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain why broilers kept in a warm house gain mass efficiently.

points.description: Little movement and warm surroundings mean less energy is used for movement / keeping warm (less heat lost)
So more of the energy in the feed is used for growth (converted to body mass)

parts.explanation: In a warm house the birds move little and lose little heat, so less of the energy in the feed is used up and more goes into growth.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Give **two** disadvantages of rearing chickens in this way.

points.description: Any one: welfare concerns (crowding, stress, little natural behaviour) / disease spreads quickly
Any other one: routine antibiotics may lead to resistant bacteria / waste and smell / energy used for heating and lighting / feed (grain) could be eaten by people

parts.explanation: Disease spreads quickly among crowded birds, and the birds have little room to behave naturally.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Why does Tendai disinfect visitors' boots and limit who enters the house?

options.content: To keep the birds calm so that they eat more and grow faster
options.rationale: Calm birds are good, but this does not explain disinfecting boots.

options.content: To stop the birds escaping
options.rationale: Disinfecting boots does not affect escapes.

options.content: To keep the house warm by keeping the door shut
options.rationale: Disinfection is about pathogens, not temperature.

options.content: To keep out pathogens, as disease spreads fast among crowded birds
options.rationale: Biosecurity keeps out pathogens that could infect the whole flock.

explanation: Feed per kilogram gained $= 3.6 \div 2.1 = 1.71... \approx 1.7\ \text{kg}$. Warmth and little movement mean less energy is lost, so more becomes body mass; but crowding raises welfare and disease problems, so farms use strict hygiene.
workedSolution:
**(a)** $3.6 \div 2.1 = 1.714... = 1.7\ \text{kg}$ of feed per kg gained (2 s.f.).

**(b)** Less energy used in movement and keeping warm → more energy for growth.

**(c)** Welfare; disease spread; antibiotic resistance; waste; energy use.

**(d)** Biosecurity: disease spreads quickly in crowded birds.
hints: Divide the feed eaten by the mass gained.

stem: Plant breeders want a maize variety for farmers in Masvingo Province, where the rains are often short and unreliable.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Which feature should the breeders select for?

options.content: Early maturity, so the crop finishes before the rains end
options.rationale: A crop that matures quickly is less likely to be caught by drought late in the season.

options.content: Very tall plants that need a long growing season to ripen
options.rationale: A long season increases the risk of drought before harvest.

options.content: Large leaves that lose a lot of water
options.rationale: This would make drought damage worse.

options.content: Grain that ripens only after heavy rain
options.rationale: Heavy rain is not reliable in this region.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Describe how the breeders would use selective breeding to produce the new variety.

points.description: Choose parent plants that show the feature (e.g. mature early / survive dry spells)
Cross-breed (pollinate) them and grow the offspring
Select the offspring that show the feature best and breed from them
Repeat over many generations

answerSpec.markingNotes: Any three points, one mark each, to a maximum of 3.

parts.explanation: Choose parents that mature early or survive dry spells, cross them, grow the seed, select the best offspring and breed from those, repeating for many generations.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Suggest **one** risk if every farmer in the region grows the same new variety.

points.description: Little genetic variation, so a new disease or pest could destroy most crops at once

parts.explanation: With little genetic variation, a new disease or pest could spread through all the farms and destroy most of the crop.

explanation: Selective breeding chooses parents with a useful feature (early maturity), breeds them and selects the best offspring over many generations. Growing one variety everywhere reduces genetic variation, increasing the risk from a new disease.
workedSolution:
**(a)** Early maturity.

**(b)** Choose parents → cross → select best offspring → repeat for many generations.

**(c)** Low genetic variation: one disease could wipe out the crop.
hints: What would let a crop escape a short rainy season?

stem: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of growing crops such as maize or tobacco as large-scale monocultures. [6]

points.description: Advantage: efficient use of machinery and methods / fast planting and harvesting with few workers
Advantage: large, uniform harvest, cheaper to produce and suited to processing and markets
Disadvantage: loss of habitats and reduced biodiversity (woodland or grassland cleared)
Disadvantage: pests and diseases spread and build up, so more pesticides are used (harming other species; resistance)
Disadvantage: soil depletion, so more fertiliser is needed, with runoff polluting water / soil erosion when bare
A reasoned conclusion, e.g. monocultures feed many people cheaply, but their harm can be reduced by crop rotation, integrated pest control and keeping areas of natural vegetation

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Monocultures are efficient. One set of machinery and one method can be used over the whole farm, so planting, spraying and harvesting are quick and need few workers. The harvest is large and uniform, which suits processing and selling and makes food cheaper.

However, clearing natural woodland or grassland for one crop destroys habitats and reduces biodiversity. A huge area of one plant lets its pests and diseases spread and build up, especially if the crop is grown every year, so more pesticides are used; these harm pollinators and the natural enemies of pests, and pests may become resistant. The same mineral ions are removed every year, so more fertiliser is needed, and runoff can pollute rivers and dams. Bare soil after harvest is easily eroded.

Overall, monocultures produce a lot of food cheaply, but their harm can be reduced by rotating crops, using integrated pest control and leaving strips of natural vegetation.

explanation: A discussion needs both sides and a conclusion. Marks come from specific points: efficiency and cheap uniform harvests against biodiversity loss, pests and pesticides, and soil and water damage.
hints: Give at least two advantages and three disadvantages, then a conclusion.

stem: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of intensive livestock production, such as broiler houses, piggeries and cattle feedlots. [6]

points.description: Advantage: animals move little and are kept warm, so less energy is lost and more food is converted into meat, eggs or milk
Advantage: less land is needed / products are cheaper and available all year / conditions are easy to control and monitor
Disadvantage: welfare concerns: crowding, stress, little natural behaviour
Disadvantage: disease spreads quickly; routine antibiotics may produce antibiotic-resistant bacteria
Disadvantage: concentrated waste pollutes water (eutrophication) and causes smells / energy used for heating and lighting
Disadvantage: animals eat grain and soya that people could eat, so energy is lost along the food chain

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Intensive units produce food efficiently. The animals move little and are kept warm, so less of the energy in their food is used for movement and keeping warm, and more becomes meat, eggs or milk. Little land is needed, conditions are easy to control, and products are cheap and available all year.

On the other hand, crowding causes stress and prevents natural behaviour, which raises welfare concerns. Diseases spread quickly, so antibiotics are often used routinely, which can lead to antibiotic-resistant bacteria. Large amounts of manure collect in one place and can pollute rivers, and heating and lighting use a lot of energy. The animals are fed grain and soya that people could eat, so energy is lost along the food chain.

Intensive farming feeds many people cheaply, but it should be balanced against animal welfare and environmental harm.

explanation: Balance the efficiency gains (energy, land, cost) against welfare, disease and antibiotic resistance, pollution and energy losses.
hints: Use energy ideas for the advantages.

stem: A farmer sprays a **selective** herbicide over her whole maize field. Why does this not kill the maize?

options.content: It kills broad-leaved weeds but not grasses such as maize
options.rationale: Selective herbicides affect some kinds of plant more than others.

options.content: Maize leaves are waxy, so no herbicide reaches their cells
options.rationale: Selective herbicides are chosen for the kind of plant they kill, not because the crop avoids the spray.

options.content: The herbicide only kills plants that have flowers
options.rationale: Maize has flowers too (tassels and silks).

options.content: The maize breaks the herbicide down into useful fertiliser
options.rationale: Maize does not turn herbicide into fertiliser.

explanation: Selective herbicides kill broad-leaved weeds but leave narrow-leaved grasses, such as maize, wheat and sugar cane, largely unharmed, so the whole field can be sprayed.
